newsitem.title: UK: EU gas directive impact seen marginal in UK.
newsitem.headline: EU gas directive impact seen marginal in UK.

text.p: The proposed European Union Gas Directive will have only a marginal economic impact in Britain and may have a negative effect, Clare Spottiswoode, Director General of Gas Supply, said on Thursday.
Giving evidence to the House of Lords European Communities Committee, Spottiswoode said the directive may have some minor benefits in Britain, but it was just as likely the impact would be negative.

This is because long-term take-or-pay contracts may be renegotiated or derogated after the directive is approved, and such contracts favour producers. As a large producer, Spottiswoode said, Britain has more to lose than gain from any change to take-or-pay contracts.

But she added that Ofgas, the industry regulator, was working with the Department of Trade and Industry (DTI) to support the directive and to explain it to other EU governments, companies and civil servants "really purely because it's a good idea."

Giles Chichester, European People's Party MEP and a member of the European Parliament's Research, Technological Development and Energy Committee, earlier told the committee that he felt the directive was likely to be approved before the end of this year during the Luxembourg presidency of the EU.
"I have high hopes the Luxembourg Presidency have put it at the top of their list of priorities and may be able to strike a compromise," he said.

The gas directive is intended to liberalise gas markets, enabling customers to buy gas from a range of suppliers. Under a proposal put forward by the Dutch presidency, the market was to be opened in three stages. First, users of over 25 million cubic metres a year (mcm/yr) or more would get the right to buy gas competitively.
This would then fall in a second stage to users of 10 mcm/yr, before coming down to all users of over 1 mcm/yr in a third stage.

These thresholds have now been withdrawn from the current draft of the directive. Chichester said he believes the thresholds are "pathetically underambitious," and advocates opening the market to all consumers in the final stage - as will be done in Britain by June next year.

But Spottiswoode was more sanguine about the exact level of thresholds. "I'm not sure that it matters," she said. "The key thing is that there should be something there that's going to be introduced."
She also said it did not matter up to what date take or pay contracts should continue to be valid.

Lord Geddes, chairman of the committee, said several witnesses had told the committee it was important that take-or-pay contracts should be guaranteed only if they had been signed by a certain date. But some said this should be 1996, others said January 1994, and one said it should be no later than 1992 and could be as early as 1998.
"The prize would be any date, as long as it's not in the future as some European countries are asking for," Spottiswoode replied.
